hero.headline: Trump to decide today on Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
hero.body:
President Trump has issued an aggressive deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, threatening military action if the waterway remains closed. In profanity-laden posts on his Truth Social platform, Trump gave Iran until Tuesday at 8 p.m. Eastern Time to open the strait or face destruction of Iranian power plants and bridges.

"Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran," Trump wrote. "Open the Fuckin' Strait, you crazy bastards, or you'll be living in Hell."

The ultimatum comes as US officials confirmed that the United States and Iran have agreed to a framework for a deal. A senior Iranian source acknowledged that an understanding has been reached but is not yet finalized. The tentative agreement would extend a ceasefire and establish new nuclear talks between the two countries.

Despite his threats, Trump told Fox News on Sunday that there is a "good chance" of reaching an agreement with Iran quickly. "If they don't make a deal and fast, I'm considering blowing everything up and taking over the oil," he said.

The strait represents a critical global shipping route for oil. Iran has gained leverage in the conflict by threatening and attacking vessels passing through the waterway, creating pressure on international energy markets. Oil prices surged following Trump's threats, with West Texas Intermediate crude rising to more than $112 a barrel and Brent climbing above $110.

Trump has repeatedly extended his deadline for Iran to reopen the strait, shifting it from Monday to Tuesday in his latest announcement. Iranian officials have acknowledged that messages have been exchanged between the two countries through intermediaries including Pakistan, though Tehran insists it has not formally entered peace negotiations.

Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of Iran's parliament, responded to Trump's threats on social media. "Your reckless moves are dragging the United States into a living HELL for every single family, and our whole region is going to burn because you insist on following Netanyahu's commands," he wrote. "The only real solution is respecting the rights of the Iranian people and ending this dangerous game."

Trump's language drew criticism from US lawmakers. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said on X: "Happy Easter, America. As you head off to church and celebrate with friends and family, the President of the United States is ranting like an unhinged madman on social media. He's threatening possible war crimes and alienating allies."

International law experts have raised concerns about the legality of targeting civilian infrastructure. Oona Hathaway, a professor of international law at Yale University, stated that the threatened attacks would constitute war crimes under the Geneva Conventions, saying that "immiserating the civilian population for bargaining leverage is not lawful."

cards.headline: Israeli Forces Cross Into Lebanon Beyond Litani River
cards.teaser: Israeli military operations expanded across a key river in Lebanon, with five people killed in the advance.
cards.body:
Israeli forces crossed the Litani River in Lebanon as part of an expanded ground offensive. Prime Minister Netanyahu confirmed that soldiers moved across the river and that the air force was operating in Beirut and the Bekaa Valley. The crossing represents an expansion of Israeli military operations in Lebanese territory.

Five people were killed in Lebanon during the operations. The Litani River has historically served as a significant boundary in southern Lebanon. Israeli strikes have continued despite ceasefire arrangements, according to reports documenting ongoing military activity in the region.

cards.headline: US sanctions Lebanese officials over Hezbollah ties
cards.teaser: The Treasury Department targeted nine individuals including parliamentarians and Lebanese Army Intelligence officers for serving the militia's security operations.
cards.body:
The sanctions included Hezbollah parliamentarians, Amal Movement security figures, and Lebanese Army Intelligence officers. The action signals that state positions no longer provide immunity if the individual serves the militia's security structure.

The Treasury Department said the designations target people who support Hezbollah's operations despite holding official government roles. The sanctions represent an expansion of US efforts to separate Lebanese state institutions from the armed group.

cards.headline: United Arab Emirates Conducted Airstrikes on Iran During War
cards.teaser: The UAE carried out dozens of strikes against Iran alongside the US and Israel, according to a new report.
cards.body:
The United Arab Emirates carried out dozens of airstrikes against Iranian targets during the recent war and following the truce, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal. The operations involved coordination with both the United States and Israel, revealing a previously undisclosed military role for the UAE in the conflict.

The strikes mark a significant expansion of the Emirates' military involvement in regional tensions with Iran. The coordinated nature of these operations demonstrates the interconnected military responses among the three countries during this period.

cards.headline: SEC Moves to Eliminate Climate Disclosure Rule for Public Companies
cards.teaser: The Securities and Exchange Commission proposed ending a regulation that would have required publicly traded companies to disclose climate-related risks.
cards.body:
The Securities and Exchange Commission proposed eliminating a climate change disclosure rule that would have applied to all publicly traded companies. The regulation would have required companies to disclose whether they faced significant risks from climate change and its effects.

The proposal represents a reversal of the disclosure requirement before it took effect. Public companies would no longer be mandated to report climate-related risks to investors under the proposed change to SEC regulations.

cards.headline: Trump Administration Allows Companies Tax Breaks Through Overseas Havens
cards.teaser: U.S. companies avoided at least $40 billion in taxes using arrangements in Malta, Bermuda, Cyprus and other locations since early 2025.
cards.body:
The Trump administration cleared the way for companies to avoid taxes through arrangements in overseas locations including Malta and Cyprus. U.S. companies skirted at least $40 billion in taxes since the beginning of 2025 using schemes in places like Malta, Bermuda and Cyprus.

The policy change enables companies to use tax haven structures that reduce their U.S. tax obligations. The $40 billion figure represents tax revenue that was avoided through these international arrangements over roughly a year and a half.

hero.headline: Russian Drone Hits Romanian Apartment Building, Injuring Two Civilians
hero.body:
A Russian drone struck a residential apartment building in the Romanian city of Galați during an overnight attack on Ukraine, wounding two people and prompting swift international condemnation. Romanian authorities said the drone was likely intercepted by air defenses over Ukraine before altering course and entering Romanian airspace.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte responded quickly to the incident, stating that the alliance is "ready to defend every inch" of its territory. "Russia's reckless behaviour is a danger to us all," Rutte wrote on social media following a call with Romanian President Nicuşor Dan.

The drone crashed into the roof of a residential building in Galați, a city on the Danube River west of Romania's borders with Ukraine and Moldova. The impact sparked a fire and forced the evacuation of several residents. Emergency services responded to the scene, and Romanian military forces scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and a helicopter authorized to engage targets.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu stated that the country would formally communicate consequences for Russia's actions and pursue next steps at the European level regarding sanctions. The foreign ministry described the incident as a "grave and irresponsible escalation" and a serious breach of international law. It also announced plans to request that NATO accelerate the transfer of anti-drone capabilities to Romania.

Romanian officials indicated they would invoke Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which allows member nations to request consultations when their security is threatened. This mechanism differs from Article 5, which addresses collective defense against armed attack.

President Dan convened an emergency meeting of Romania's supreme council of national defense and instructed the foreign ministry to prepare a package of measures regarding Romania's relationship with Moscow. He emphasized that Romania would not accept the war being transferred to its citizens.

Russian President Vladimir Putin denied involvement, suggesting without evidence that the drone might have been a Ukrainian weapon. He requested that drone wreckage be handed over to Russia for independent investigation.

The incident drew condemnation from European leaders. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia's "war of aggression has crossed yet another line" and pledged full solidarity with Romania. France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot also denounced what he called an "irresponsible act by Russia."

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident demonstrated that Russian aggression poses a threat to all of Europe and the Black Sea region.

This strike represents another example of the war in Ukraine spilling across borders, adding to growing concerns about Russia's wider campaign of hybrid warfare across Europe.

cards.headline: Fire at Kenyan Police School Dorm Kills 16 Students
cards.teaser: Authorities arrested eight students following a fire at a school run by Kenya's police that left 16 dead.
cards.body:
A fire tore through a dormitory at Utumishi girls academy in Gilgil, Nakuru county—about 76 miles northwest of Nairobi—just after midnight on Thursday, killing at least 16 students. The blaze swept through the facility at the girls' school in Kenya's Rift valley region.

Kenya's education minister said eight students were arrested in connection with the fire. They could face charges next week, according to the minister's statement.

cards.headline: United Nations Adds Israel and Russia to Sexual Violence Blacklist
cards.teaser: The UN placed both Israel and Russia on its annual list of parties committing sexual violence in conflict zones.
cards.body:
The United Nations added Israel and Russia to its annual blacklist of parties credibly documented to have committed sexual violence during armed conflict. Israel's inclusion relates to alleged sexual violence by Israeli forces against Palestinian detainees, while Russia's designation concerns documented incidents in conflict areas.

Israel responded swiftly to the decision, announcing it would cut ties with the UN chief. The annual blacklist identifies armed groups and state forces with documented patterns of sexual violence in conflict zones.

cards.headline: Canadian Man Admits to Aiding Suicides Through Online Chemical Sales
cards.teaser: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to charges related to selling toxic chemicals to people who used them to end their lives.
cards.body:
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to 14 counts of assisting suicide after mailing "suicide packets" containing lethal chemicals to more than 100 people across dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, the US, Italy, Australia, and New Zealand. He appeared in court in Newmarket, Ontario, where prosecutors withdrew 14 murder charges in exchange for his guilty plea.

While Law admitted to charges relating to Canadian victims, families of the deceased are calling for additional charges in the United Kingdom, where 79 deaths have been linked to his sales. Sentencing is scheduled for September.

cards.headline: Trump Says He Will Decide on Iran Proposal Soon
cards.teaser: The president said he was meeting with advisers about Iran's response to his conditions for negotiations.
cards.body:
President Trump is meeting with advisers at the White House to make a final determination on an Iran deal. According to officials, the US and Iran have agreed on a framework for a potential agreement. Trump has stated that Iran must meet his longstanding conditions as part of any deal.

The discussions come as the administration works through the details of the proposal with Tehran. Trump is expected to announce his decision following these internal consultations with his team.

cards.headline: Five killed, 34 injured in bus crash on I-95 in Virginia
cards.teaser: A bus hit six vehicles on Interstate 95 southbound in Stafford County, killing five people and injuring dozens more.
cards.body:
A bus crashed into six vehicles on Interstate 95 southbound in Stafford County, Virginia, killing five people. State police said 34 people were injured in the crash.

The collision involved the bus and six other cars on the highway. The crash closed the southbound lanes of I-95 in the area.

cards.headline: Judge blocks payouts from Trump's $1.776 billion settlement fund
cards.teaser: A federal judge temporarily halted work on President Trump's anti-weaponization settlement fund as a lawsuit proceeds.
cards.body:
A federal judge in Virginia temporarily blocked the Trump administration from transferring money into a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund. The order from US District Judge Leonie Brinkema on Friday prevents the government from taking any further action in creating or operating the fund while a legal challenge proceeds.

The two-page order aims to ensure no funds are irreversibly disbursed from the fund before the court can hear additional legal arguments in the case challenging it.

cards.headline: Louisiana passes congressional map eliminating majority-Black district
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers voted to dismantle one of two majority-Black congressional seats after the Supreme Court ruled the current map unconstitutional.
cards.body:
Louisiana's Republican lawmakers moved quickly to redraw the state's congressional districts after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the existing map unconstitutional. The new map reduces majority-Black districts from two to one.

The Republican-controlled legislature acted rapidly to implement the change following the court's sweeping ruling on the issue.

cards.headline: Kenyan court blocks US plan for American Ebola quarantine facility
cards.teaser: A court in Kenya suspended US plans to build a quarantine facility for American Ebola patients in the country.
cards.body:
A Kenyan court blocked the United States plan to establish a quarantine facility in Kenya for American Ebola patients. The proposed facility sparked opposition both in Kenya and in the United States.

US officials said Americans who contract Ebola will now be sent to Europe for treatment instead of the United States. The Kenyan court suspended plans for the Ebola quarantine unit after local resistance to the proposal.

cards.headline: Drivers changing habits as gas prices remain high
cards.teaser: Consumers are going out of their way to find discounts at the pump as fuel costs stay elevated, according to retailers.
cards.body:
High gas prices are prompting drivers to change their shopping habits in search of better deals at the pump. Major retailers like Costco and Walmart have reported increased consumer interest in discounted fuel options, with customers adjusting their routines to access lower prices.

The situation may worsen ahead. Oil executives have cautioned that gas prices could rise further in the coming months, potentially intensifying pressure on household budgets already strained by broader inflation concerns.

cards.headline: Attacks on Ebola clinics linked to distrust of medical workers
cards.teaser: Community members are attacking treatment facilities and distrusting doctors during the outbreak, echoing patterns from past epidemics.
cards.body:
Community members are attacking Ebola clinics and distrusting medical workers during the current outbreak in Congo. The pattern echoes previous epidemics, with attacks driven by concerns around trust, death, and body bags.

Local burial traditions are compounding the problem. Because community members continue following these practices rather than accepting medical guidance, cases of Ebola spread further. This distrust of doctors and treatment facilities has significantly hindered containment efforts. The WHO chief traveled to Congo's capital to assess the response to the rare Ebola outbreak amid ongoing insecurity and community resistance.

hero.headline: Blue Origin Rocket Explodes on Florida Launch Pad During Test
hero.body:
A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded on a launch pad at Cape Canaveral in Florida on Thursday night during a scheduled test, dealing a significant blow to the company's space ambitions and potentially disrupting NASA's lunar timeline.

The explosion occurred at 9pm ET during a "hotfire" test at Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 36. A massive fireball engulfed and destroyed the launchpad, with the blast visible from extraordinary distances. An orange sky was reported in Fort Pierce, roughly 115 miles to the south, while residents in South Carolina hundreds of miles away reported seeing a glow in the sky. The shockwaves were felt across Florida's Atlantic coast, causing homes to shake in nearby Cape Canaveral and Cocoa Beach.

Blue Origin confirmed that all employees were safe and uninjured. Jeff Bezos, the company's founder, described it as a "very rough day" on social media, stating the company was already investigating the cause. "It's too early to know the root cause but we're already working to find it," Bezos wrote. "We'll rebuild whatever needs rebuilding and get back to flying. It's worth it."

The explosion creates serious complications for NASA's ambitious plans. Just two days earlier, NASA announced that Blue Origin had won a contract to launch the first of three planned uncrewed lunar missions this year to begin construction of a $20 billion moon base. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the agency would conduct a full evaluation of that timeline following the incident, which Blue Origin described as "an anomaly."

"Spaceflight is unforgiving, and developing new heavy-lift launch capability is extraordinarily difficult," Isaacman wrote. "We will work with our partners to support a thorough investigation of this anomaly, assess near-term mission impacts, and get back to launching rockets."

The New Glenn rocket is critical to NASA's Artemis program. It will be used to launch landers to the moon, including the landers that will carry astronauts to the lunar surface. Blue Origin is also competing with SpaceX for contracts to provide lunar landers for the Artemis IV mission planned for 2028, which would mark the first crewed lunar landing since 1972.

This explosion represents the latest in a series of setbacks for Blue Origin. Last month, a payload from the third flight of New Glenn ended up in the wrong orbit, leading the Federal Aviation Administration to temporarily ground the rocket. Thursday's test was the first static fire test since the FAA cleared it to return to flight the previous week.

Flames were still burning at the launchpad more than two hours after the explosion. Emergency officials said there was no threat from fumes or other potential hazards.

cards.headline: Dell Shares Jump 30% as AI Server Demand Drives Strong Quarterly Results
cards.teaser: Dell's stock price surged after the computer maker reported results powered by artificial intelligence server sales and price increases.
cards.body:
Dell shares rose 30% following strong quarterly earnings results, adding $34 billion to founder Michael Dell's personal wealth. The stock surge reflects investor confidence in the company's financial performance and market position.

The gains were driven by robust demand for AI servers as companies invest heavily in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Dell's results exceeded Wall Street expectations, with the company capitalizing on the broader artificial intelligence boom that is reshaping the technology sector.

cards.headline: Stock Indexes Reach Record Highs as S&P 500 Heads for Ninth Weekly Gain
cards.teaser: Major stock market indexes hit new all-time highs, with technology stocks leading gains and oil prices declining.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 and other major stock indexes reached new all-time highs, with the S&P 500 on track for its ninth consecutive weekly gain. Technology stocks led the advance, with Dell posting strong results following positive earnings.

Oil prices declined as investors evaluated ongoing international negotiations. The combination of robust technology sector performance and lower energy costs drove broad-based gains across major indexes.

cards.headline: Oil Prices Decline as U.S. and Iran Near Potential Agreement
cards.teaser: Oil markets dropped as investors weighed signs of a possible deal to extend a cease-fire between the United States and Iran.
cards.body:
Oil prices fell as the United States and Iran moved closer to a potential agreement. Investors assessed tentative signs of a pact to extend a cease-fire between the two countries.

Stock markets fluctuated alongside oil prices as traders evaluated the implications of the possible diplomatic agreement. The prospect of an extended cease-fire influenced energy market pricing and broader financial markets.

cards.headline: Train Fire at Penn Station Injures Five, Disrupts Rail Service
cards.teaser: A maintenance train caught fire at Penn Station, injuring five people and causing service disruptions for NJ Transit, Amtrak and LIRR.
cards.body:
A fire in a rail yard train car near Penn Station injured five people early Friday, disrupting service across multiple transit systems. The fire, which occurred in an Amtrak car in the Hudson River tunnel, damaged overhead wires and caused delays on New Jersey Transit and Amtrak services into New York.

Long Island Rail Road service was briefly suspended due to the incident, coming just over a week after a strike had shut down that system. The fire affected commuters at one of the country's busiest transit hubs, causing widespread delays across the regional rail network.

hero.headline: ClickUp cuts 22% of workforce as tech layoffs surge in 2026
hero.body:
Productivity software company ClickUp eliminated 22 percent of its workforce to replace positions with AI agents, according to Box founder Aaron Levie. The cuts add to a wave of technology sector job losses that have brought 2026 layoffs nearly level with the entire previous year despite only five months passing.

Levie described the decision as an example of what he termed AI psychosis. He argued that executives authorizing AI replacements for human workers often have limited understanding of what those jobs actually require. The comment highlights growing tension over how companies evaluate which roles artificial intelligence systems can perform.

Tech industry layoffs have accelerated sharply in 2026. The pace of job cuts through late May rivals the total number recorded across all of 2025, suggesting companies are moving quickly to restructure operations around AI capabilities.

ClickUp makes project management and collaboration software used by businesses to coordinate work. The company had not previously announced major workforce reductions. Representatives did not provide details on which departments or roles were eliminated or how the AI agents would handle the work previously done by human employees.

The software industry has seen multiple rounds of layoffs since 2023 as companies adjusted to slower growth and higher interest rates. The current wave differs in that many companies explicitly cite AI adoption as a reason for reducing headcount rather than general economic conditions.

Levie founded Box, a cloud storage and collaboration company, in 2005. He has become an active voice in debates over AI implementation in business settings. His criticism focused on a disconnect between executive decision-making and operational reality, suggesting leaders may overestimate AI capabilities while underestimating the complexity of human work.

Other technology companies have announced plans to integrate AI agents into operations but most have not specified job cuts as a direct result. ClickUp's approach represents one of the most explicit substitutions of AI for human workers publicly disclosed so far.

The broader pattern reflects how companies across industries are responding to artificial intelligence development. While some organizations have announced workforce reductions citing other factors, the technology sector has been at the forefront of companies directly linking headcount cuts to AI implementation.

Industry observers note that the speed and scale of these changes raise questions about whether companies are adequately preparing for the transition. The debate between executives who see AI as a clear path to efficiency gains and critics like Levie who question whether leadership fully understands the implications continues to intensify as more companies follow ClickUp's lead.

cards.headline: Groq seeks $650 million in funding after Nvidia deal
cards.teaser: The AI chip startup is raising new capital as it shifts focus toward AI inference software.
cards.body:
AI chipmaker Groq is raising $650 million in internal funding as it transitions from hardware development to AI inference services—the process of optimizing how AI models respond to user requests.

The fundraising follows Nvidia's $20 billion arrangement with Groq, which involved acquiring the startup's specialized chip technology and talent. Groq had previously built chips designed to accelerate AI workloads before shifting its strategic focus toward software-based inference solutions.

cards.headline: Microsoft threatens security researcher with criminal investigation
cards.teaser: A public dispute between the company and an independent researcher has reignited debate over software security responsibility.
cards.body:
Microsoft threatened an independent security researcher with criminal investigation over the disclosure of security vulnerabilities in its products. The public dispute has reignited debate within the security community about the appropriateness of such legal threats against researchers who identify flaws.

The confrontation highlights a longstanding tension between software companies and outside researchers. It raises questions about who bears responsibility for securing software and whether legal intimidation is an effective strategy for managing vulnerability disclosures.

cards.headline: Startup offers free home cleaning in exchange for robot training footage
cards.teaser: A company is paying humans to wear head cameras while cleaning houses to collect data for training robots.
cards.body:
A startup is offering free home cleaning services to customers willing to have the work recorded by head-mounted cameras, with the footage used to train robotic systems. The arrangement represents the latest approach to gathering human demonstration data for machine learning.

The company provides cleaning at no cost while collecting video of how humans navigate homes and perform cleaning tasks. This data trains robots to replicate human movements and decision-making. The model extends existing practices where workers wear cameras in various settings to create training datasets for automation systems.

cards.headline: Cognition founder says AI coding agents should assist, not replace programmers
cards.teaser: Scott Wu, whose company makes Devin, stated the AI tool is designed to work alongside human developers.
cards.body:
Scott Wu, founder of Cognition, has stated that AI coding agents like Devin are designed to support human programmers rather than replace them. Devin, described as the first and most successful AI coding agent in commercial use, can write code and complete software tasks autonomously.

Wu's position comes amid growing discussion about AI's impact on programming jobs. His stance contrasts with some companies that have reduced developer headcount while expanding their use of AI tools.

cards.headline: Severed sea cucumber tissue continues living without dying
cards.teaser: Researchers found that amputated sea cucumber appendages reorganize and persist indefinitely.
cards.body:
When sea cucumbers lose appendages, the severed tissue doesn't simply die as would be expected. Instead, the amputated parts reorganize their tissues and continue functioning independently. Scientists have observed this remarkable ability to persist, with some separated tissue remaining viable for years after detachment from the original organism.

This phenomenon suggests a form of biological resilience that challenges typical patterns of cell death. Rather than degrading, the severed appendages demonstrate a capacity to maintain themselves in ways that researchers have described as showing tendencies toward immortality.

cards.headline: Study suggests pigeons may navigate using their liver on cloudy days
cards.teaser: New research proposes that pigeon livers could act as magnetic field sensors for navigation.
cards.body:
A study published recently suggests homing pigeons may use their liver to sense Earth's magnetic field when navigating on cloudy days. Researchers propose the organ could function as a compass mechanism, though other scientists have expressed skepticism about the findings.

The research addresses a longstanding question about how pigeons find their way home across long distances when they cannot rely on the sun for orientation. The liver hypothesis offers a potential explanation for navigation during overcast conditions, but the mechanism would require biological processes not yet fully demonstrated in birds.

hero.headline: Four-time Stanley Cup champion Claude Lemieux dies at 60
hero.body:
Claude Lemieux, a four-time Stanley Cup champion, died Thursday at age 60. Authorities reported that Lemieux died by suicide.

Lemieux had a distinguished 21-season NHL career, establishing himself as one of hockey's most dominant playoff performers. He won Stanley Cup titles with the Montreal Canadiens, the New Jersey Devils twice, and the Colorado Avalanche.

During his playing career from 1983 to 2003, Lemieux played for seven different NHL teams. He appeared in more than 1,200 regular season games and scored over 380 goals across his time in professional hockey.

One of Lemieux's greatest achievements came in 1995 when he earned the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP. That year, he led the Devils to their first Stanley Cup championship, scoring 13 goals during the postseason. He became known for his physical style of play and his knack for scoring crucial goals in elimination games, making him a valuable asset during playoff runs.

Lemieux came from a hockey family and passed his passion for the sport to his son Brendan, who also played in the NHL. His influence extended beyond his own achievements, as he helped foster the next generation of hockey talent.

The four Stanley Cup championships he won placed Lemieux among a select group of players who achieved sustained success across multiple teams and extended periods. His career spanned an era when the NHL expanded and grew significantly in popularity throughout North America.

Lemieux's playing style and competitive intensity made him a memorable figure in professional hockey. His success in playoff situations demonstrated his ability to perform when the stakes were highest, earning respect from teammates, opponents, and fans alike.

The hockey community is mourning the loss of a championship-caliber player whose impact on the sport extended well beyond his statistics. His contributions to multiple Stanley Cup-winning teams left a lasting legacy in NHL history.

Authorities have not released additional details about the circumstances surrounding his death. The tributes from the hockey world have focused on Lemieux's postseason performances and his place among the game's great champions. His death marks the loss of a significant figure from a transformative period in professional hockey's history.

cards.headline: Knicks center Mitchell Robinson to play in NBA Finals Game 1 after hand surgery
cards.teaser: Robinson plans to play while wearing a hand brace after undergoing surgery for a broken pinkie finger.
cards.body:
Mitchell Robinson will take the court for the Knicks in Game 1 of the NBA Finals despite recently undergoing surgery on his broken right pinkie finger. The center plans to wear a protective brace on his hand during the championship series opener.

The decision keeps New York's starting center available for the finals, with Robinson protected by specialized equipment as he returns to play.

cards.headline: Baseball labor battle begins as league pushes for salary cap
cards.teaser: Major League Baseball and its players union are at odds over a potential salary cap as collective bargaining negotiations start.
cards.body:
Major League Baseball is pushing for a salary cap as collective bargaining agreement negotiations begin. The MLB Players Association is opposing the proposal.

The disagreement marks the opening of what could become a contentious labor negotiation between the league and its players. Baseball has operated without a salary cap throughout its modern era, unlike other major professional sports leagues in North America.

cards.headline: French Open player faces sanction after saying match needed male umpire
cards.teaser: Adolfo Daniel Vallejo argued that his match official was not strong enough to control the crowd.
cards.body:
Paraguayan player Adolfo Daniel Vallejo is facing a significant sanction from French Open organizers after criticizing umpire Ana Carvalho during his second-round match. Vallejo argued that the experienced Brazilian official was unable to control the crowd and that a man should have been assigned to the match instead.

Vallejo lost to French teenager Moïse Kouamé in a competitive four-hour-plus match on Court Suzanne Lenglen. The crowd, largely composed of French supporters backing the home player, was described by Vallejo as "very out of line." Tournament officials announced they would impose disciplinary action against Vallejo for his comments about the umpire's ability to manage the match.

cards.headline: Paige Bueckers debut jersey sells for record $64,720
cards.teaser: The jersey from the Dallas Wings star's first WNBA game set a record price for a WNBA jersey.
cards.body:
Paige Bueckers' Dallas Wings jersey from her WNBA debut on May 16, 2025, sold for $64,720 through MeiGray, setting a new record for a WNBA player jersey. The authentication company and marketplace handled the transaction.

The sale price reflects the exceptional interest surrounding Bueckers' arrival in the league as one of the most anticipated rookies in WNBA history.

cards.headline: Luka Doncic invests in Rome basketball team with NBA Europe bid
cards.teaser: The Mavericks star is teaming up with a former Dallas executive to bring professional basketball to Rome.
cards.body:
Luka Dončić is partnering with former Dallas Mavericks executive Donnie Nelson on a basketball venture in Rome. The group has submitted a bid to join the NBA Europe league, which the league is currently developing.

The project represents the NBA's push to expand its presence in European markets, with Rome serving as a potential hub for professional basketball in Italy's capital.

cards.headline: Tennis player retires from French Open after tripping on advertising board
cards.teaser: Zeynep Sonmez had to withdraw from her doubles match after the courtside accident.
cards.body:
Zeynep Sönmez was forced to retire from her doubles match at the French Open on Friday after tripping over a courtside advertising board while chasing a ball during play.

The incident occurred as the player pursued a shot near the edge of the court, resulting in her withdrawal from the match.

hero.headline: More Than Half of Freedom 250 Performers Drop Out Amid Political Backlash
hero.body:
At least seven of the nine featured musical acts scheduled to perform at Freedom 250, a concert series marking the United States' 250th anniversary, have withdrawn from the event within 48 hours of the lineup being announced. The festival, organized by the Trump administration and set to take place in Washington, D.C., has faced significant challenges in maintaining its roster of performers.

Bret Michaels became the latest artist to back out on Friday, citing a deteriorating atmosphere surrounding the event and threats being made against performers. His withdrawal follows similar decisions by other musical acts who were originally committed to the multi-day concert series.

The exodus of performers reflects broader tensions within the entertainment industry regarding political associations. Musicians face difficult decisions when weighing professional opportunities against potential backlash from their fan bases and advocacy groups. Those dropping out have cited both political concerns and direct threats as reasons for their withdrawals.

A spokesperson for Freedom 250 has maintained that the festival contains nothing partisan in its nature, despite the clear political connections that have prompted artists to distance themselves from the event. The statement came as organizers continued to lose performers from their planned lineup.

The concert series was originally envisioned as a large-scale celebration featuring musical acts across multiple days. However, the Trump administration's involvement has proven problematic for booking talent. Artists who initially agreed to participate have faced public criticism and pressure from fans and various advocacy organizations.

The festival's difficulties in retaining performers mirror previous incidents where musicians have withdrawn from politically charged events. The Trump connection has become a defining characteristic of Freedom 250's public image, overshadowing the original vision for what was intended to be a national celebration. As performers continue to distance themselves from the event, significant questions remain about whether organizers can assemble adequate programming for the planned concerts.

Major news outlets including The Washington Post, Politico, NBC4 Washington, and Vanity Fair have reported on the wave of cancellations. The scale of the performer exodus has drawn attention from multiple media sources tracking the controversy surrounding the event.

The situation highlights how political affiliations can create substantial obstacles for entertainment events seeking mainstream participation. Even as organizers insist the festival maintains no partisan agenda, the withdrawal of multiple high-profile musical acts suggests that artists and their representatives view the political dimensions as significant enough to warrant stepping back from their commitments.

cards.headline: Damien Leone Partners With Sam Raimi on New Horror Film for Lionsgate
cards.teaser: The creator of the Terrifier franchise is working with Sam Raimi on a new horror project called Tortures of the Damned.
cards.body:
Lionsgate acquired Tortures of the Damned, the next horror film from Damien Leone, known for creating the Terrifier series and the character Art the Clown. Sam Raimi is partnering with Leone on the project, though the studio and filmmakers have not revealed plot details.

Leone built his reputation making low-budget horror films. His Terrifier franchise gained a cult following for its intense horror elements and practical effects work.

cards.headline: Netflix Adds Shalom Brune-Franklin and Jimmy O. Yang to Oscar Isaac Vegas Drama
cards.teaser: Two actors have joined the cast of The Roman, a Las Vegas casino drama series starring Oscar Isaac.
cards.body:
Shalom Brune-Franklin and Jimmy O. Yang are joining the cast of The Roman, a Netflix drama series set in Las Vegas. Oscar Isaac stars in the show, which centers on the casino industry.

Brune-Franklin, known for roles in Dune: Prophecy and Sunny Dancer, will play Jessica Christine JC Griffin. The character is described as an ambitious rising star working at the casino.

cards.headline: Rafael Nadal Documentary Tracks Tennis Star's Path to Retirement
cards.teaser: A four-part Netflix series follows Rafael Nadal's final years in professional tennis before his 2024 retirement.
cards.body:
Filmmaker Zachary Heinzerling created a four-part Netflix docuseries titled Rafa that documents Rafael Nadal's journey to retirement in 2024. The series offers extensive access, featuring interviews with Nadal, his wife, coaches, and opponents throughout his career.

Nadal retired at age 38 after winning 22 Grand Slam titles, including 14 French Open championships that earned him the nickname King of Clay. Heinzerling, who previously directed Stolen Youth: Inside the Cult at Sarah Lawrence, captures Nadal's transformation from his early years as an athletic, charismatic player to his decision to step away from professional tennis.

cards.headline: CSI Creator Develops AI-Generated True Crime App
cards.teaser: Anthony Zuiker is creating Cinemalistics, an application that uses artificial intelligence to produce true crime content.
cards.body:
Anthony Zuiker, who created the CSI franchise, is developing an AI-generated true crime app called Cinemalistics. David Freeman, a former digital media chief at CAA who now runs startup Kynetic Media Ventures, approached Zuiker about creating a real-time true crime project roughly six months ago.

Zuiker declined to pursue another vertical video format for the project. Freeman left his role at the talent agency to found Kynetic Media Ventures before reaching out to Zuiker about the collaboration.

cards.headline: Milli Vanilli Freedom 250 Performance Status Unclear
cards.teaser: Conflicting reports surround whether Milli Vanilli will perform at the Trump-backed festival, complicated by competing versions of the group.
cards.body:
Fab Morvan, one of the original members of Milli Vanilli, says he is performing at the Freedom 250 festival in Washington, D.C. However, conflicting reports surround the booking, with some indicating the group was never approached or booked for the event.

The confusion is compounded by competing versions of Milli Vanilli operating in 2026. The Trump-backed festival has attracted scrutiny over its political associations.

cards.headline: Actors Learning New Languages for Emmy-Nominated Roles
cards.teaser: Multiple performers in this year's Emmy race acquired new language skills specifically for their television roles.
cards.body:
A trend has emerged among actors competing for Emmy nominations: learning entire new languages for their parts. Several performers developed language abilities beyond perfecting accent work for their roles in recent television productions.

The shift represents an expansion beyond traditional accent coaching. Actors submitted performance reels that showcase their ability to speak languages they did not previously know, demonstrating a commitment to authenticity in their portrayals.

hero.headline: Federal judge blocks Trump anti-weaponization fund
hero.teaser: A federal court temporarily halted the administration's $1.776 billion fund to compensate people claiming wrongful government targeting.
hero.body:
U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema issued a temporary order Friday barring the Trump administration from taking any further action on a $1.8 billion settlement fund. The order prevents the Department of Justice from transferring money into or operating the fund while legal challenges proceed.

The fund was designed to compensate people who claim they were wrongfully targeted by the government. The judge's decision ensures no funds are irreversibly disbursed while the case continues.

cards.headline: Louisiana passes congressional map eliminating Black majority district
cards.teaser: The state legislature approved a new map that removes Rep. Cleo Fields's seat after a Supreme Court ruling struck down the previous map.
cards.body:
Louisiana's Republican-controlled legislature passed a new congressional map Friday that eliminates one of the state's two Black-majority districts. The map, which runs from Shreveport to Baton Rouge, was redrawn after the U.S. Supreme Court recently ruled the previous map unconstitutional.

The new redistricting plan favors Republican representation by reducing Black voting power in Louisiana's congressional delegation. The legislature approved the map with a 28-10 vote, moving quickly to implement changes following the Supreme Court's decision.

cards.headline: JFK Airport begins Ebola screenings for Central and East Africa travelers
cards.teaser: Enhanced screenings started at New York's airport for passengers arriving from countries affected by the ongoing Ebola outbreak.
cards.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Thursday that John F. Kennedy International Airport would begin the enhanced screenings at 11:59 p.m. that night. The measure targets travelers from nations in Central and East Africa experiencing outbreaks.

The airport was added to a list of facilities conducting health screenings for the disease. The CDC implemented the protocols as part of efforts to prevent the virus from entering the United States through international travel.

cards.headline: US sanctions Lebanese officials over Hezbollah ties
cards.teaser: The Treasury Department targeted nine individuals including parliamentarians and Lebanese Army Intelligence officers for serving the militia's security operations.
cards.body:
The sanctions included Hezbollah parliamentarians, Amal Movement security figures, and Lebanese Army Intelligence officers. The action signals that state positions no longer provide immunity if the individual serves the militia's security structure.

The Treasury Department said the designations target people who support Hezbollah's operations despite holding official government roles. The sanctions represent an expansion of US efforts to separate Lebanese state institutions from the armed group.

cards.headline: Pentagon recruiting troops for White House UFC events
cards.teaser: Internal messages show military personnel must pay their own way and meet physical requirements to attend fights at the White House.
cards.body:
The Pentagon is recruiting service members to attend UFC fights at the White House, according to internal memos obtained by The Post. Participating military personnel are required to cover their own attendance costs.

The recruitment effort includes strict physical requirements that troops must meet to be eligible. The initiative appears aimed at filling audience seats for mixed martial arts events hosted at the executive mansion.

cards.headline: Speaker Johnson's chief of staff departing in early June
cards.teaser: Hayden Haynes, one of Mike Johnson's longest serving aides, will leave his position as the Speaker's top staffer.
cards.body:
Haynes started as campaign manager when Johnson first ran for Congress in 2016. He became chief of staff once Johnson took office and remained in the role when Johnson became Speaker.

The departure marks a significant staff change for the Republican leader. Haynes was among Johnson's most trusted advisers throughout his congressional career and ascent to the speakership.

cards.headline: Drag performer Pattie Gonia speaks out on Patagonia trademark dispute
cards.teaser: The entertainer urged the outdoor apparel company to drop its lawsuit over the stage name.
cards.body:
Drag queen Pattie Gonia is challenging a trademark lawsuit filed by Patagonia, the outdoor apparel company founded in 1973. According to the performer, Patagonia claims she violated an agreement by using the company's branding in merchandise.

Pattie Gonia has called on Patagonia to drop the legal action. The dispute centers on the similarities between the performer's stage name and the company's brand identity.
